newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp News Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp News Update.

text.p: COSTELLO SAYS COMMENTS NOT AN ASSESSMENT
Federal Treasurer Peter Costello says his comments about U.S. inflation and interest rate policy were simply his assessment of what the indicators show.
Mr Costello's comments about his meeting with the U.S. Federal Reserve chief Alan Greenspan, caused a stir on global financial markets.
The Treasurer says his comments weren't an assessment of what Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan is thinking.
He's received support from Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer, who says the difficulties caused for Australia by the comments should be kept in perspective.
And Mr Fischer's rejected calls for Mr Costello's resignation.
BEAZLEY RENEWS DEMAND FOR COSTELLO RESIGNATION
Federal Opposition leader Kim Beazley says Treasurer Peter Costello appears to be in denial, after revealing details of his conversation with the Chairman of the U.S. Federal Reserve Allan Greenspan.
Mr Costello's comments on U.S. inflation and the outlook for U.S. interest rate policy have prompted a strong reaction on world financial markets.
But when questioned this morning, Mr Costello denied giving his assessment of Mr Greenspan's thinking.
On Sydney Radio 2UE, Mr Beazley renewed his demand for Mr Costello's resignation.
INVESTIGATION INTO CHEMICAL IMPORTS
An investigation into the quality of chemical imports is about to be launched to determine whether Australia's agricultural sector or environment are under threat.
The National Registration Authority's Ben Sellinger says there is some question about the quality of chemicals coming into Australia from companies which don't hold the patent for their manufacture.
Mr Sellinger says European and American imports have generally been OK, but some problems are emerging with cheaper, imitations made in Asia.
He says there are two levels of possible harm in using the cheaper imports.
The first is damage to crops or animals, the second is occupational or environmental damage.
HANSON OFF TO THE TERRITORY
Controversial Federal Independent MP Pauline Hanson will visit the Northern Territory in three or four weeks time.
The Member for Arnhem, John Ah Kit, says arrangements are being made for Ms Hanson to look at Aboriginal living conditions in Central Australian communities.
Mr Ah Kit says time restraints will prevent Ms Hanson from visiting Top End communities.
FLU DRUG COULD BE READY IN TWO YEARS
A drug to effectively combat the flu virus could be available within two years.
On the final day of the 56th-Anzaas Congress in Canberra, Doctor Graham Laver from the Australian National University, said clinical trials on the drug GG167 were already underway.
Doctor Laver's work has been partly responsible for the development of GG167 and he says wide distribution could stop another flu pademic.
LIVING WAGE CASE TO BE HEARD IN DECEMBER
The Full bench of the Industrial Relations Commission has ordered that the Living Wage case be heard in December, rejecting calls by employer groups to delay the case.
Employers had argued that the case should be held over until after the Federal Government's Workplace Relations Bill was passed.
However, the ACTU said the Commission should deal with the law as it stands, not wait for new laws to be passed.
ACTU Secretary, Bill Kelty says the decision is a win for the union movement.
TEST CASE COULD OPEN THE WAY FOR OTHER CLAIMS
The Queensland Government could be open to claims amounting to tens of millions of dollars, following a Human Rights Commission finding.
The Commission has found the work practices by the Government between 1975 and 1984 were discriminatory and asked it to pay six Aboriginal elders seven thousand dollars each in compensation.
Commissioner Bill Carter found the Government was discriminatory in not paying award wages to the Palm Island elders in North Queensland, wholly and solely beacuse they were Aborigines.
He found it was quite impossible to assess the complaints in isolation from the historical background, but it's estimated thousands were affected.

The case is being seen as a test for other Aboriginal people who were subject the same government policies on other reserves. But the finding also limits claims by the relatives and spouses of those affected by the policy, with Commissioner Carter dismissing a claim by widow Florence Coutts, who's husband Buller Coutts died during the decade long legal battle.
REITH CONFIDENT IR BILL WILL BE HAPPENING NEXT YEAR
Industrial Relations Minister, Peter Reith, says he's getting closer to getting agreement with the Democrats on the Government's legislation, while there's no time-table for finalising the talks.
In Brisbane to address the Queensland Working Womens' Service, Mr Reith said he's very confident that the bill will be through the Senate and the legislation will start next year.
Meanwhile, eighty community-based organisations, headed by the Australian Council of Social Service, have urged the Senate to amend the Government's laws to protect the vulnerable.
The groups have called on the Opposition, Democrats, and independants to ensure the bill doesn't leave the young, low paid and part-time employees worse off.
STONE STARTS TO SELL STATEHOOD
Northern Territory Chief Minister Shane Stone says a Federal Private Members Bill aimed at overturning the Territory's voluntary euthanasia law, highlights the need for total independence.
Mr Stone has begun a public campaign to sell the benefits of statehood to Territorians.
He spoke to more than 300 Country Liberal Party members last night, and hopes other planned meetings will encourage the public to contribute to the debate.
